author: fatlosscoachivan
caption: Common fitness and bodybuilding myths—busted with science and facts: 💪 Top Fitness & Bodybuilding Myths — BUSTED 1. Myth: "Lifting weights makes women bulky." Truth: Women don’t have enough testosterone to build bulky muscle easily. Lifting weights actually tones, strengthens, and improves body composition. ✅ Lifting promotes fat loss and improves metabolic rate. ❌ Bulky muscles come from intense training, specific diets, and often supplements—not casual gym workouts. 2. Myth: "You need to train every day to see results." Truth: Muscles grow during rest, not just workouts. Recovery is crucial for muscle repair and growth. ✅ Aim for 3–6 sessions/week with rest or active recovery days. ❌ Overtraining can lead to injury, fatigue, and burnout. 3. Myth: "You can spot reduce fat (like doing crunches to lose belly fat)." Truth: You can’t target fat loss in specific areas with exercises. ✅ Fat loss happens overall through a calorie deficit. ❌ Hundreds of crunches won’t burn belly fat unless your diet supports fat loss. 4. Myth: "Cardio is the best way to lose fat." Truth: Cardio helps, but diet and strength training are more effective long-term. ✅ Weight training boosts metabolism and preserves muscle mass. ❌ Excess cardio can lead to muscle loss if not balanced with resistance training and proper nutrition. 5. Myth: "More sweat = better workout." Truth: Sweating is your body’s way of cooling down—not an indicator of fat burned. ✅ Intensity and effort matter more than sweat. ❌ You can have a killer workout with little sweat depending on environment and workout type. 6. Myth: "Protein shakes are necessary to build muscle." Truth: Protein is necessary—shakes are just a convenient source. ✅ Whole foods like chicken, eggs, fish, and beans work just as well. ❌ Supplements are not magic—they don’t replace training or diet. 7. Myth: "Muscle turns into fat if you stop working out." Truth: Muscle and fat are two different tissues. One doesn’t turn into the other. ✅ If you stop training and overeat, muscle mass can decrease and fat can increase. ❌ The muscle doesn’t “transform” into fat—it atrophies. 8. Myth: "You need to feel sore after every workout for it to work." Truth: DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) isn’t a measure of workout effectiveness. ✅ Progress = getting stronger, building muscle, improving endurance. ❌ Soreness can mean you did something new—not necessarily something better. 9. Myth: "You need to eat every 2–3 hours to keep your metabolism high." Truth: Meal frequency has little effect on metabolism. ✅ Total daily calories and macros are what matter most. ❌ You can eat 2 or 6 times a day and get the same results—if nutrition is on point. 10. Myth: "If you stop training, all your gains disappear immediately." Truth: Muscle loss is gradual. You don’t lose it overnight. ✅ Muscle memory helps you regain it faster when you return. ❌ A few missed workouts or even a week off won’t erase progress. #fitnessmyths #gymtips #nutritiontips

author: patrick_lyons
caption: Debunking more Exercise Myths 😤💪🏼 By this point, it’s clear the fitness world has no shortage of myths that sound good on social media but don’t survive contact with actual data. Here are some more common misconceptions that deserve to be retired once and for all. Myth 1: You have to stretch before every workout. Static stretching before training can actually decrease strength and power output for up to an hour afterward. A proper warm-up should instead raise your heart rate, activate key muscles, and prepare your joints for movement. Save static stretching for after training or on rest days (PMID: 17194255). Myth 2: More gym time means more results. Training longer can get you more gains, but isn’t necessary and it isn’t always better. The vast majority of muscle growth and strength improvements happen from high-quality, focused work, usually in under 60–90 minutes. Overtraining without adequate rest can blunt progress and increase injury risk (PMID: 22235613). Myth 3: Machines are only for beginners. Machines aren’t “easy mode.” They’re tools that can help isolate weak points, safely load muscles to failure, and maintain tension throughout the range of motion. Many elite bodybuilders and powerlifters strategically use machines alongside free weights for maximum development (PMID: 28599036). Myth 4: You need soreness to prove you worked hard. Soreness is just inflammation from unfamiliar movement, not a badge of effectiveness. Once your body adapts to a routine, soreness will decrease even as strength and muscle continue to grow. The goal is progress, not pain (PMID: 29178369). Myth 5: You can’t build muscle while losing fat. While difficult, it’s absolutely possible, especially for beginners, people returning after time off, or those with higher body fat. With adequate protein, resistance training, and a small calorie deficit, you can build muscle and lose fat simultaneously (PMID: 28422575). The truth? Sustainable progress isn’t about doing more; it’s about doing smarter.  Train with purpose, rest with intention, and stay consistent.  Myths complicate what’s simple: stimulus, recovery, and time build results. If you’re serious about turning your fitness goals into reality, spots are available on the Lyon Shred. author: fitzonehealthsolutions
caption: You can eat the same food… and accidentally track completely different calories depending on whether you weigh it raw or cooked 😳🍚 This is one of the biggest reasons women say: “I’m in a calorie deficit but I’m not losing weight.” Because 100g of uncooked rice is NOT the same as 100g of cooked rice. 100g of raw chicken is NOT the same as 100g of cooked chicken. 100g of dry pasta is NOT the same as 100g once it’s boiled. When food cooks, it can absorb water, lose water, shrink, expand, or change weight dramatically. The calories don’t magically disappear… but your portion measurement can get completely thrown off if you’re using the wrong entry in your calorie tracker. 🤯 For example: dry rice absorbs water and gets heavier after cooking. So if you log “100g rice” but choose the dry/raw entry while weighing cooked rice, you could be logging way more calories than you actually ate. But with meat, it often loses water while cooking and becomes lighter. So if you weigh cooked chicken but log it as raw chicken, your calorie and protein tracking can be off too. 🍗 And those little “off” measurements add up fast: breakfast + lunch + dinner + snacks = suddenly you’re not in the calorie deficit you thought you were. If your goal is fat loss, weight loss, losing belly fat, or getting back into your favorite jeans… consistency matters more than perfection. 💪✨ Pick ONE method: 🥩 Weigh raw food and log raw entries 🍚 OR weigh cooked food and log cooked entries Just don’t mix them. This is especially important for women over 30 trying to lose weight, busy moms trying to meal prep, and women in the USA who are tired of “eating healthy” with no results. You do not need to starve. author: primetrain
caption: **BLIND RANKING THE BEST TRAINING SPLITS 💪** People massively overcomplicate training splits. The best split isn’t the one that looks coolest on paper. It’s the one that lets you train hard, hit enough quality volume, recover properly and actually stay consistent. 🥇 **Upper / Lower / Push / Pull / Legs — 5 days** My favourite if building muscle is the main goal. Plenty of volume, good frequency and enough recovery without living in the gym. 🥈 **Push / Pull / Legs / Full Body — 4 days** Elite option. Three focused sessions, then a full-body day to hit everything again. 🥉 **Upper / Lower x2 — 4 days** Probably all most people need. Simple, balanced and gives you heaps of recovery. 4️⃣ **Full Body x3 — 3 days** Massively underrated. If you’re busy, this is one of the best ways to still hit everything multiple times each week. 5️⃣ **Push / Pull / Legs x2 — 6 days** It works, but six days is a lot if you’re genuinely training hard. Recovery becomes the issue. 6️⃣ **Arnold Split x2 — 6 days** Great sessions, but again, six days is a big commitment and probably unnecessary for most people. 7️⃣ **Bro Split — 5 days** It can absolutely build muscle, but smashing one muscle with heaps of volume then waiting a full week to train it again isn’t how I’d personally structure things. The big thing though… Your split matters WAY less than: 📈 Progressive overload 🔥 Hard working sets 🎯 Quality volume 😴 Proper recovery 🤝 Consistency You can build muscle on almost any split if those things are dialled in. caption: 🏪 COMMENT ”711“ for the full tier list ranking all the popular snacks and gave my own personal recommendations. I ranked 7-Eleven protein options by actual value, not just the word “protein” on the label.  The formula is simple: High protein, low calories, low cost. Because a drink can have amazing macros, but if it costs $6 every time, it may not be the best everyday option. The biggest surprise? Hanjuku eggs came in last. A lot of people think eggs = high protein, but whole eggs are only around 40% protein weightage, and at $3, the value is not great compared to other options. For my vegan friends, NutriSoy Protein is still a solid convenience pick. $2.60 for 20g protein, easy to drink, easy to find. The trending Protee drink is insane for protein-to-calorie ratio, 20g protein for only 85 calories, almost 90% protein weightage. But because it costs around $6, it doesn’t win on value. Chobani is a good middle ground if you want something solid and filling. Meiji High Protein is still one of the strongest overall picks, especially when there’s a promo. But the winner for value? 7-Eleven chicken breast. High protein, low calories, affordable, and when the 2 for $4 promo is on, it becomes almost unbeatable. So if you’re trying to hit protein while cutting, don’t just buy the most “fitness-looking” product. Look at the full picture: protein, calories, cost, and how filling it actually is. caption: This ranking is based on my own experience, coaching results, and personal preference when dieting for fat loss. When calories drop, protein sources are not equal. What matters most is protein density, satiety, and calories per serving. Some foods deliver a high amount of protein with very few calories, making it much easier to stay in a deficit while preserving muscle mass. Others technically contain protein but bring a lot of extra fats or carbohydrates that reduce efficiency during a cutting phase. When you’re trying to lose body fat without losing muscle, the goal is simple: maximize protein while minimizing unnecessary calories. That’s why lean, highly satiating protein sources tend to work best during aggressive fat loss phases. This isn’t about “good vs bad foods.” It’s about efficiency when cutting. author: nolan.labuda
caption: You did not gain a pound of fat overnight…Here’s what really happened 👇 Let’s do the math first: •	1 lb of fat ≈ 3,500 calories. •	If your maintenance is 2,500 calories/day, you’d need to eat ~6,000 calories in one day just to POSSIBLY gain 1 lb of fat. •	That means one extra meal, dessert, or night out isn’t enough to instantly add a pound of fat. So why does the scale spike so quickly? 1️⃣ Water Retention (the biggest reason): •	Carbs are stored as glycogen in your muscles and liver. •	For every 1g of glycogen, your body stores ~3g of water. •	High-carb meal → glycogen fills up → water is pulled in → scale goes up. •	This is why you look fuller and more pumped after eating carbs. 2️⃣ Food Volume: •	Extra food is still in your stomach and intestines. •	Until it’s digested and processed, it shows up as “weight.” 3️⃣ Sodium & Bloating: •	A salty meal makes your body retain water. •	Once hydration balances out, the scale normalizes. 4️⃣ Training-Related Inflammation: •	Hard workouts increase muscle glycogen storage and cause fluid shifts. •	Your body sends fluid to repair and recover → temporary water weight → scale rises. 5️⃣ Hormonal Fluctuations: •	Women: cycle changes can swing the scale by 3–5 lbs. •	Men & women: stress hormones like cortisol also cause water retention. ⚡️ The Truth: The scale measures everything (water, food, glycogen, inflammation)…not just fat. Fat gain requires consistent overeating over time — not one night out. 👉 Next time you wake up heavier, don’t panic. It’s usually water, food, or recovery…not fat.
